ratings.reviewer_notes: SFB acquisition directly links a gut microbe that expands intestinal Th17 cells with impaired skeletal maturation, but IL-17 itself is not measured or causally tested.
Directly demonstrates that dysbiotic microbiota transfers osteoporosis through a decanoic acid–Th17–IL-17A pathway; IL-17A blockade and microbiota/B. pseudolongum interventions alleviate bone loss.
In an inflammatory bone-loss model, DCA reverses dysbiosis, lowers IL-17 and other inflammatory mediators, and improves bone architecture, supporting a testable gut–IL-17–bone hypothesis.
L. rhamnosus reduces Th17 cells and IL-17 while attenuating ovariectomy-induced bone loss, but gut dysbiosis or microbiome-composition changes are not assessed.

Gut microbiome depletion simultaneously reduces intestinal IL-17 expression and partially rescues bone loss in sickle-cell mice, supporting a microbiome–inflammation–bone pathway, though IL-17 is not independently blocked.
Shows microbiome-dependent expansion and trafficking of intestinal Th17 cells, increased bone-marrow IL-17, RANKL activation, and bone loss; blocking T-cell trafficking prevents bone loss.
Directly connects SFB-enriched microbiota to intestinal Th17 expansion and migration to bone marrow in PTH-induced bone loss, providing a mechanistic gut microbiome–Th17/IL-17–bone framework.
L. acidophilus lowers Th17 cells, IL-17, and RANKL while protecting bone in ovariectomized mice, but dysbiosis and microbiome changes are not directly characterized.
Human case-control study identifies gut microbial dysbiosis associated with primary osteoporosis, but provides no IL-17 or Th17 evidence and no causal mechanism.

In colitis-associated osteoporosis, probiotic treatment changes gut microbiota, suppresses IL-17 and intestinal inflammation, and improves bone microarchitecture, supporting an integrated hypothesis despite no selective IL-17 blockade.
Treatment corrects ovariectomy-associated gut dysbiosis, reduces Th17/IL-17 responses, and mitigates bone loss, directly supporting a testable microbiota–immune–bone relationship.
Human evidence associates increased Th17 frequency and IL-17 with low bone mineral density, but the gut microbiome or dysbiosis is not investigated.
Establishes a causal role for IL-17 in estrogen-deficiency bone loss through neutralization experiments and osteoclastogenic signaling, but does not examine gut microbiome dysbiosis.
